texts: Jules Verne wrote "The Divine Comedy" in the early 1860s, shortly after he had completed his initial works like "A Journey to the Center of the Earth". Inspired by Dante Alighieri's intricate journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise, Verne took a detour from his usual science fiction themes to explore a more fantastical and allegorical narrative. The novel was a significant departure from his typical style, reflecting a period of experimentation in his literary career.

Jules Verne did not write "The Divine Comedy." "The Divine Comedy" is a work of literature written by the Italian poet Dante Alighieri in the 14th century. It is a long narrative poem that consists of three cantiche (or books): "Inferno," "Purgatorio," and "Paradiso."

Jules Verne, on the other hand, was a French author who lived in the 19th and early 20th centuries. He is best known for his works of science fiction, such as "Journey to the Center of the Earth," "Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea," and "Around the World in Eighty Days." Verne's works are often characterized by their imaginative and futuristic themes, and they have had a significant influence on the science fiction genre as a whole.

Jules Verne wrote "The Divine Comedy" in 1878. After gaining fame with his pioneering science fiction works, Verne turned to exploring the themes of the afterlife and human morality. His rendition of "The Divine Comedy" captivated audiences with its vivid imagination and intricate descriptions, blending elements of his visionary storytelling with the allegorical journey originally envisioned by Dante. Verne’s version, uniquely set within his time's understanding of science and technology, was serialized in French literary magazines before being published as a full volume the following year.
